overview: This bill, the Tule River Tribe Reserved Water Rights Settlement Act of 2025, approves a settlement of long-running water rights claims by the Tule River Tribe of central California, signed in 2007 by the tribe and two groups of downstream water users. It confirms the tribe's right to use up to 5,828 acre-feet of water a year from the South Fork of the Tule River (an acre-foot is enough to cover an acre of land one foot deep), held in trust by the federal government and protected from being lost through non-use. It provides $518 million, adjusted for construction costs, for tribal water projects such as storage, treatment and pipelines, including $20 million for studies of a planned reservoir, plus $50 million for upkeep, and it places about 9,000 acres of nearby national forest land and several parcels of Bureau of Land Management land into trust as part of the reservation. In exchange, the tribe and the United States as its trustee give up other water rights claims covered by the settlement, and the deal takes effect only after a federal court approves it and all the money is provided. As of May 12, 2025, a Senate committee had approved it and it was placed on the Senate calendar.
for: Supporters say it ends decades of legal uncertainty over water rights, gives the tribe a reliable water supply and the means to build it, and protects downstream users' existing rights.
against: Critics say it commits more than half a billion federal dollars, with further increases tied to construction costs, and transfers thousands of acres of public forest land out of general public management.
